In All Code Is Slop (Except Mine) — Lauren Tan, SpaceXSI, Lauren Tan ("Potato") explains how she scaled from shipping 3,000 personal pull requests a month [00:42] to her team shipping 11,000 PRs a month without sacrificing software quality [13:34]. Her core thesis is that AI coding agents allow any developer to operate like an elite "coding machine," shifting the software engineer's primary job toward designing deterministic guardrails and verification systems so agents produce reliable code by default [01:04].

1. Core Thesis: Trust Through Environment Design
Productivity without quality loss: With coding agents, raw code volume is no longer the bottleneck; the real challenge is maintaining or improving code quality while scaling output [01:04].

Engineered trust over blind trust: Running a "software factory" relies on investing upfront in the agent's environment—a process that took Tan about six months to refine—so you can trust agents to do the right thing automatically [01:25].

2. The Inverse Pyramid of Agent Guardrails
Tan organizes environment investments into four layers, prioritizing deterministic code constraints at the bottom and minimizing natural-language instructions at the top [01:57]:

The codebase itself (Deterministic): Strong API design, clear architecture, and proactive refactoring form the primary foundation [02:04].

Static analysis and testing (Deterministic): Lint rules, type systems, compilers, and automated test suites constrain what agents can write and force good patterns by default [02:13].

Verification (Runtime and formal): Runtime checks and formal proofs uncover subtle bugs, enforce system invariants, and confirm the agent understood your actual intent [02:28].

Prose (Minimal top layer): Markdown rules, skills, and agents.md files should be kept small and reserved only for areas requiring genuine human judgment [02:42].

3. Codebase as a Garden & Concrete Engineering Rules
Inputs dictate outputs: Because the existing codebase is an agent's largest input, every agent correction should be converted into a deterministic code check rather than another line in a prompt or agents.md file [02:59].

Tending the garden: As PR velocity jumps from a handful per day to hundreds, code arrives like a continuous living stream [03:33]. Architectural constraints act as concrete foundations [04:03], whereas tech debt, workarounds, and anti-patterns act like weeds that agents immediately copy and spread—requiring engineers to keep the codebase pristine [04:25].

Banning high-nuance APIs: Tools that require deep nuance to use safely inevitably lead to agent "slop" [05:24]. In Dune (a Next.js-like client framework built for Electron apps), Tan's team banned React's useEffect in product code—allowing it only inside controlled framework APIs—which categorically eliminated a whole class of code review issues [04:58].

Enforcing architecture via directory structure: To stop agents from importing Electron main-thread code into the renderer thread (which causes UI jank) [06:15], they split code into explicit electron-renderer and electron-main top-level directories and blocked cross-imports with lint rules and a dependency graph analyzer [06:30].

Banning 99% of code comments: Agents frequently use markdown files and inline comments to rationalize hacks or over-rotate on minor feedback [07:00]. For example, an architectural mismatch between VS Code's imperative style and React's declarative style previously led agents to spam timers (setTimeout, requestAnimationFrame, requestIdleCallback), triggering heavy garbage collection lag while writing comments defending the workarounds [07:28]. Tan's team banned 99% of comments—because they go stale and cannot be enforced—and replaced them with descriptive lint errors that instruct agents to fix the root cause [08:17].

Shrinking human code review: Systematically converting review feedback into lint rules and cleaner APIs steadily removes manual review bottlenecks until agents can safely merge most of their own pull requests [09:08].

4. Verification & The Golden Age of Testing
Reviewing artifacts instead of diffs: Code review shifts toward inspecting verification artifacts such as videos, screenshots, diagrams, and formal proofs [09:44].

Runtime verification with feature maps and CLIs: Agents run and debug the app directly using tools like the Chrome DevTools Protocol [10:06]. A user-facing feature map (acting like a UI sitemap) gives agents shared vocabulary for interface components, while reusable custom CLIs inside agent skills reduce token consumption and improve reliability [10:06].

Formal verification and property-based UI testing:

TLA+: Used for model checking complex user flows, such as multi-device notifications [10:52].

Lean: Used to mathematically prove critical algorithms, such as ensuring a custom virtualization library has zero flickering or jitter [11:05].

Bombadil: Used for property-based UI testing to catch subtle interface bugs [11:40].

The economics of verification: Echoing industry observations that roughly 70% of daily tokens now go toward verification [11:51], Tan notes that agents make historically expensive testing and formal methods cheap enough to use routinely—sparking a "golden age of software testing and verification" [12:23].

Visualizing state machines: Tan built a state-chart skill (in her psac / potato stack plugin) to generate user-facing state machine diagrams that can be reviewed alongside videos and screenshots [12:59].

5. Production Results & Outer-Loop Automation
Real-world throughput and stability: Using these practices, the Graphbot team shipped 11,000 pull requests in one month, cuts daily stable releases, and onboarded 227 contributors in October—including casual contributors with minimal prior context [13:26]. Meanwhile, the PR revert rate dropped to roughly 0.5% [14:15], and core Electron app metrics (startup, typing, and chat switching) grew faster than at launch [14:31].

Fix the inner loop before automating the outer loop: Automating a sloppy coding loop only generates faster, more expensive slop [15:12]. Once static checks and verification foundations are solid, teams can orchestrate outer-loop automation—such as automatically spinning up Cursor cloud agents on every new release to fuzz the build like a real user, open fix PRs, and automerge them [16:07].

# Moneo Desktop native backend

`index.ts` replaces `docker-compose.yml` inside the desktop app: PostgreSQL, GoTrue, PostgREST and the
Storage API run as child processes on `127.0.0.1`, behind a small gateway with the same three paths as
`docker/Caddyfile`. The binaries come from `node scripts/desktop/fetch-backend.mjs` (pinned versions and
SHA-256 in that script), and land in `desktop/.build/` (in a package, `resources/`).

## Home folder

| Path | What |
| --- | --- |
| `config.json` (0600) | generated secrets (same generation as `scripts/setup.mjs`), preferred ports, setup state |
| `postgres/` | the cluster (`initdb -U supabase_admin`, UTF8, ICU en-US, scram-sha-256) |
| `storage/` | Storage API files |
| `data/`, `workflow/` | `MONEO_DATA_DIR`, `WORKFLOW_LOCAL_DATA_DIR` for the app |
| `backups/<time>-<reason>/` | `database.dump` (pg_dump -Fc), `storage/`, `config.json`, `manifest.json` |
| `logs/` | `backend.log`, `auth.log`, `rest.log`, `storage.log`, `postgres/` |
| `run/services.json` | PID and executable of each running service, so a start after a crash can end leftovers |

## After a crash or force-quit

- `pg_ctl` starts Postgres outside the app's process tree, so it keeps running. At the next start,
  a `postmaster.pid` whose PID is alive and is a `postgres` executable from this bundle (or one whose
  command line names this data folder) is stopped with `pg_ctl stop -m fast`; any other PID there means
  the file is stale and it is deleted.
- GoTrue and PostgREST: on Windows they end with the app (libuv puts children in a kill-on-close job);
  elsewhere they may survive. At the next start each PID in `run/services.json` is ended only if it is
  alive, its executable is the recorded one and lies inside the bundled backend. Nothing is matched by
  name, and a PID now used by another program is left alone.
- The Storage server exits by itself within a second once the process that started it is gone
  (`MONEO_PARENT_PID`, checked by a few lines fetch-backend.mjs puts at the top of its bundle).

## Start order

1. Postgres (`initdb` on first run, otherwise the recovery above), via `pg_ctl`.
2. First run only: `desktop/bootstrap/*.sql` as `supabase_admin`, then the passwords and JWT settings
   `docker/db/roles.sql` sets.
3. Refuses to go on if the database has a migration newer than the bundled ones. With pending
   migrations (or other bundled service versions) on an existing database: an automatic
   `pre-upgrade` backup (the newest 5 automatic backups are kept).
4. GoTrue (runs its migrations), Storage API (runs its migrations), PostgREST, gateway.
5. `supabase/migrations` exactly like `scripts/setup.mjs` (same `supabase_migrations.schema_migrations`,
   one transaction per file, `notify pgrst`), then the owner through the GoTrue admin API.

## Differences from the Docker backend

- **safeupdate** is compiled from pinned upstream source against each bundled PostgreSQL and
  preloaded for `authenticator`, preserving rejection of unfiltered PostgREST updates and deletes.
  Building needs Visual Studio C++ Build Tools on Windows and a C compiler on macOS/Linux.
- **No supautils, pg_graphql, pg_net, pg_cron, pgsodium/vault, pg_stat_statements, realtime.**
  Moneo does not call these extensions; the supautils migration grants are reproduced below.
- **supautils' policy grants.** In the image, supautils lets `postgres` create and drop policies and
  triggers on `auth.*`/`storage.*` tables it does not own. Moneo's migrations need that
  (`create policy … on storage.objects`). During Moneo's own migrations only, `postgres` is granted
  `supabase_auth_admin` and `supabase_storage_admin` (`inherit true, set false`); the grant is revoked
  right after, and at every start in case a crash interrupted it. `postgres` otherwise keeps the
  image's attributes: `NOSUPERUSER BYPASSRLS`.
- **uuid-ossp** is created only where the bundled PostgreSQL has it (not in the Windows build).
- **Storage metadata on Windows.** Storage keeps content type, cache control and etag in extended
  attributes through the native `fs-xattr`, which does not exist on Windows. The bundled Storage uses
  `scripts/desktop/backend-fs-xattr-shim`: NTFS alternate data streams on Windows, the upstream
  N-API addon on macOS and Linux.
- **GoTrue on Windows** is built with a `go build -overlay` that drops one `SO_REUSEPORT` call
  (no such option on Windows); see `fetch-backend.mjs`.
- **Storage API is one esbuild bundle** (`storage-api/server.js` plus pino's three worker files,
  `migrations/`, `THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.txt`), about 16 MB instead of a 340 MB `node_modules` with paths
  over 260 characters. It runs with `EXPOSE_DOCS=false` (Swagger docs need its package.json).
- **MSVC runtime on Windows.** The Windows PostgreSQL build needs `vcruntime140.dll`,
  `vcruntime140_1.dll` and `msvcp140.dll`. They ship app-local in `postgres/bin` and `postgrest/`
  (Windows loads them from the executable's folder first), taken from Microsoft's signed
  VC_redist.x64 14.44.35211.0 and pinned by SHA-256 in `fetch-backend.mjs`, so no vc_redist install is
  needed.
- **GoTrue keeps a connection pool** (`GOTRUE_DB_MAX_IDLE_POOL_SIZE`). Its default keeps none, and on
  Windows each new Postgres connection starts a process (100+ ms), which made every page's sign-in
  check take about half a second.
- Postgres settings follow the image where they change results (`timezone = UTC`,
  `extra_float_digits = 0`, `row_security = on`, english text search); `jit = off`, no replication
  (`wal_level` default), logs rotate daily for a week.

## What changed

- **Comment ban:** a lint rule, `moneo/no-comments`, rejects every comment except tool directives such as `eslint-disable-next-line <rule> -- reason` and `@ts-expect-error`. Its error tells the agent to put the meaning in a name, type, test or lint rule, and `eslint --fix` deletes the comment.
- **Comments removed:** the subagent stripped 3,133 comments from 588 files with that autofix, with no code changes. I read "high-Q" as Haiku, so that is the model it ran on.
- **One-way imports:** `app/` → `components/` → `lib/` and `workflows/`, enforced by lint. Lint also stops `lib/finance` importing `lib/ai`, Electron imports outside `desktop/src`, and app code inside `desktop/src`.
- **Modules moved to make that true:** net-worth logic, the transaction amount parser, recurring schedules/suggestions/series, two server-action files, the chat form and the net-worth chart all left `app/` for `lib/` or `components/`.
- **AGENTS.md:** adds "never write a comment", "corrections become checks", the import layering, and a Desktop app section covering what the Electron build changes for anyone editing the code.

Not touched: comments in SQL migrations (applied migrations must not be rewritten), CSS, YAML and `.env.example`. Say if you want the non-migration ones gone too.

## What else from the talk fits Moneo

In rough order of value:

1. **Restrict `useEffect` and timers in product code.** There are 75 `useEffect` calls in 42 files and 25 timers in 19, mostly polling and auto-dismiss. Wrapping those in two or three hooks (`usePolling`, `useDismissAfter`) and banning the raw calls elsewhere is the same move as her `useEffect` ban. It is a real refactor, so I left it out of this PR.
2. **Ban `as unknown as`.** 27 uses, nearly all casting Supabase rows. Generated database types would remove them, and then a lint rule keeps them out.
3. **Screenshots and videos on the PR, not diffs.** Have Playwright attach before/after screenshots or a short recording for any changed flow, so you review what the app does.
4. **Property-based tests for money math.** `fast-check` on the `lib/finance` invariants (splits sum to the total, undo restores the exact state, currency conversion round-trips within tolerance). This is the cheap version of her Lean and TLA+ work, and it fits "financial truth comes from code".
5. **Feature map.** One generated file listing every page, widget, chat tool and command-palette entry. It would replace most of the "Hit every surface" prose with something a test can check.
6. **Outer loop, last.** The nightly browser run already exists; letting it open fix PRs on its own is the final step, once the items above are in.

Skills I would add:

- **`verify-ui`:** drives the QA server on port 3100, captures before/after screenshots in light, dark and mobile, and attaches them to the PR.
- **`review-to-rule`:** takes a review correction and turns it into a lint rule or test with a descriptive error.
- **`state-chart`:** draws the state machine for a flow (import, bank reconnect, voice call) as a diagram to review beside the screenshots.

# Browser tests

Playwright tests run against the separate test backend (Docker project `moneo-qa`, `.env.qa`) and this checkout's app on http://localhost:3100. The config starts the app with `npm run qa:server` (or a production build with `E2E_PRODUCTION_BUILD=1`) unless it is already running.

## Setup

1. Create the test backend once (and after pulling new migrations): `npm run setup -- --qa`.
2. Create the QA user and save its session: `npm run qa:auth`. Its login is stored in `.env.qa` as `E2E_USER_EMAIL`/`E2E_USER_PASSWORD`, and its session in `e2e/.auth.json` (or set `E2E_STORAGE_STATE`).
3. Before a full run, empty its workspace: `npm run qa:reset`.

The whole test backend is disposable: `docker compose -p moneo-qa down -v` and step 1 start it fresh. The owner's `moneo` project is never touched.

Tests never use the owner's workspace. Every spec runs with the saved QA session and an `x-moneo-test` header; with that header the app refuses a request that has no valid session instead of signing the owner in (`proxy.ts`). Before any spec runs, `e2e/global-setup.ts` checks that the server under test does this, so an older or foreign server on the port stops the run.

## Running

```sh
npm run test:e2e -- --workers=1
```

Use one worker: several specs change the same QA workspace and its preferences. The QA server builds into `.next-qa`, so it can run beside `npm run dev`.

## Kinds of specs

- `*.smoke.spec.ts` and `*.mocked.spec.ts` stub or skip the backend. Against a configured backend they still need the QA session, like every spec.
- `*.gated.spec.ts` need the backend. Most use the QA session; others create disposable users with the service key, sign them in by session cookie, and remove them in `finally`. If interrupted, their IDs are left in ignored `.qa/` files for cleanup.
- `*.provider.spec.ts` call the real AI model, so they cost money. They run only with `E2E_REAL_AI=1`; `npm run test:e2e` leaves them out.
- `review-runtime.config.ts` and `review-investigation.config.ts` run the real Workflow engine against local synthetic database and model servers (ports 3040/3041), including a server restart mid-review: `npx playwright test --config e2e/review-runtime.config.ts`.

## Nightly

`npm run qa:nightly -- --install` schedules the whole suite for 03:00 every day (a Windows scheduled task that starts as soon as possible if the PC was off). It runs every spec twice on a production build of `origin/main`, in its own worktree in `~/.moneo/nightly`, and keeps one GitHub issue, "Nightly browser suite is failing", up to date. A night with Docker off or port 3100 busy is skipped quietly; the log is `~/.moneo/nightly.log`.

A skipped spec is not a pass: it means a prerequisite (backend, QA session, service key) is missing.

`scalable-trading.provider.spec.ts` drives chat against a local stand-in for Scalable's MCP server (`e2e/mocks/scalable-mcp.mjs`, made-up data) with the real AI model. The three skills are added and the audit is done: [PR #223](https://github.com/indkhan/Moneo/pull/223) now carries both, and the audit's remaining suggestions are filed as [issue #224](https://github.com/indkhan/Moneo/issues/224). Lint, typecheck and unit tests (1,701, with the longer timeout) pass after the last changes; the production build last ran before the final component move, and Playwright and the desktop build were not run.

## Skills added

- **`verify-ui`**: shoot before and after pictures of every page a change touches, look at them, and put them on the PR. It uses a new command, `npm run qa:shots -- <label> home money/transactions`, which saves each page in light, dark and mobile and fails on a console error or failed request. I ran it against Home and Transactions on the QA app and it works.
- **`review-to-rule`**: turn a correction into a type, a helper plus a ban, a lint rule or a test, with an error message written for an agent.
- **`state-chart`**: read a flow's states and transitions out of the code, list the holes (failure, double tap, undo, restart), and draw it as a diagram.

Each lives in `.agents/skills/` with a pointer in `.claude/skills/`, matching `moneo-setup`.

## What the audit found in my own rules (fixed)

- **Prose could slip past the comment ban** behind any `eslint-`, `@ts-` or `@type` prefix. Directives must now match their exact form, with a reason of at most 120 characters.
- **Dynamic `import()` bypassed every boundary**, and `scripts/`, `e2e/` and root files had no rules. The boundaries are now one rule, `moneo/import-boundaries`, covering static, dynamic, re-exported, `require` and `vi.mock` paths everywhere. It immediately caught one more inverted import, so the analysis panel moved to `components/`.
- **The comment autofix could join two tokens** (`a+/*c*/+b` became `a++b`). It now leaves a space. The audit found no such case among the 3,133 removals.

## What it suggests next

All of it is in the issue, sized. The ones I would do first:

1. **Tests for three invariants that only comments used to state**: chart tooltips escape merchant names (XSS if dropped), bank errors never log the key, and the IOU loader never returns its payload.
2. **CI does not run the database or browser suites**, so the RLS, concurrency and precision checks never run on a pull request.
3. **Time zone defaults to `"Europe/Berlin"` in 8 library functions.** A caller that forgets the argument computes dates in Berlin time for every owner; making it required lets the compiler find them.
4. **Silent failures**: 52 `.catch(() => {})`, including workflow steps where a failed import ends the job with no record.
5. **One way to do things**: service-role Supabase clients are built about 12 ways, `process.env` is read in 42 files, and money is formatted in 5 places.
6. **AI tools get a read-only database type**, so "every AI write is a card" is enforced by the compiler. This is the largest item and the one closest to your goal of not reviewing.

## Two things I ran into

- **A stored setting the app does not recognise breaks every page** with "Moneo could not sign you in". The shared QA workspace had an `ai_models.default` key from another branch, and the strict settings check rejected it. # Correct

The operator keeps correcting agents in this repo for the same mistakes. Change the repo so the next agent can't make them.

Assume every contributor is an agent that sees only the files it opened, copies the nearest example, and takes the shortest path that compiles. Design the repo so a change that looks right from one file is right for the whole repo.

## Find the mistake classes

First, read recent commits, reverts, review comments, agent instruction files, and comments that explain workarounds. Group the mistakes into classes. A class counts once it has happened twice.

## Fix each class at the highest level that works

1. **Eliminate it with architecture.** Give each piece of state one owner and each task one supported way. Hide internals so the wrong import fails. Replace hand-synced lists with one source of truth. Delete old ways and dead code an agent would copy.
2. **Enforce it with types so the bad state can't be written.** If bad code still compiles, add a lint or CI check whose error names the file, type, or function to use instead. If the pattern is already common, fail only when a change adds more.
3. **Test the behavior.** Fix or delete any test that still passes when the behavior it checks breaks, or that fails when only the internals change.
4. **Write docs or agent rules last, only for judgment calls.** Nothing fails when an agent skips them.

## Fix and prove

Then fix the most frequent classes now, one commit each. Prove each new check fails on a real past mistake. Run the same command locally and in CI. Exceptions go on the offending line with a reason, an expiry date, and a human's approval.

## Keep the rule table

Last, keep a table in the agent instruction file that pairs each rule with what enforces it. When the operator corrects you, fix the mistake and add the rule. If the rule was already there and nothing enforces it, that's a repeat, so fix it at the highest level in the same change. Drop a rule once its mistake can't happen.

**Reply:** each class with its evidence, the level you picked, and why a higher level didn't work.

# Fix Root Causes

When debugging, fix the fault, not the place where it surfaced. The symptom is where a wrong state became visible. The root cause is the first place the system did something it should not do, or failed to handle a state it should handle.

**Why:** A symptom fix hides the evidence and leaves the fault free to surface somewhere else. Each one makes the system harder to reason about, because the code now carries a workaround for a bug that nobody named.

**Pattern:**
- Reproduce first.
- Ask "why" at each step until the answer is a wrong decision in the code, not a consequence of an earlier one.
- When stuck, instrument. Read the actual error and the actual state. Do not guess.
- Ask whether the state that triggered the symptom is legitimate. If the system may be in that state, the code that broke on it is the root cause, and handling the state there is the fix. If the state should never exist, a check where it broke hides the bug. Find what produced the state. Guards, retries, swallowed errors, clamped values, and discarded state are the usual ways to hide a bug.
- When something fails only after a restart, suspect persisted state first: config files, caches, lock files, serialized state.
- Check for the pattern, not just the instance. Find every place with the same fault and fix them all.
- If a workaround needs a paragraph-long comment to justify it, the code is wrong. Fix the code, not the comment.
- If the deciding fact took a deep dig to find, propose the cheap, always-on signal that would have shown it at first look.

name: principle-test-behavior-not-implementation
description: "Apply when you write, change, or keep a test. Assert what the code's users can observe, so that the test fails when that behavior breaks and keeps passing when only the internals change."
disable-model-invocation: true
---

# Test Behavior, Not Implementation

A test is a claim about what the code does for its users: a caller, an end user, or another service. Behavior is what those users can observe through the interface they use. That includes return values, errors, state they can read back, and effects on systems outside the code, such as a request sent, a row written, or a message emitted. Implementation is what they cannot observe: private helpers, internal call order, intermediate data, and which internal collaborator did the work.

Judge each test against two imagined edits:

- **Break the behavior.** Make the code return a wrong value, skip an effect, or do the effect twice. If the test still passes, it proves nothing. The usual causes are an assertion looser than the contract, an expected value computed by the code under test, a restated constant or prompt string that never runs the code that reads it, and an assertion on data that the test built itself.
- **Change the internals.** Keep every observable result the same and restructure the code underneath. If the test now fails, it is pinned to the implementation. It will need a rewrite on every refactor and still catches no bug.

Keep a test that catches the first edit and survives the second. Rewrite or delete the rest. To write a test that does both, drive the code through its users' interface with a concrete input. Derive the expected value from the requirement, not from a run of the code. Assert what the contract promises, no less and no more.

The contract decides, not the shape of the assertion. When "an empty cart never charges" is the promise, an assertion that the payment client got no call is behavior. Pair it with a case where the charge happens, so that the test shows it can see a call. The payload that a mocked external service receives is behavior, because that service observes it. A call to an internal helper is implementation, because no user can see it. An empty list is the exact answer when no record matches, and a hollow check when the test only needs some result. An exact error message pins wording that no caller reads. The error type that callers branch on is the contract.

A test can pin an invariant instead of a call, such as a key that must exist in two tables or a compile-time type check. The invariant is the behavior.

# Prove It Works

Verify every task output by checking the real thing directly. Do not infer from proxies, self-reports, or "it compiles."

**Why:** Unverified work has unknown correctness. Indirect verification (file mtimes, output freshness, agent self-reports, cached screenshots) feels cheaper than direct observation. Acting on a wrong inference costs far more than checking the source.

Check the real thing, not a proxy:
- Check process liveness directly, not indirectly through derived state
- Read the actual value, not a cached or derived representation
- When verification fails, suspect the observation method before suspecting the system

## Script the check when you can

The strongest proof is a deterministic script that re-runs the same comparison, not a one-time eyeball. Write the script, run it, and keep its output as an artifact a reviewer can re-run instead of trusting your word.

Keep the artifact visible for the human. Commit it only for large or complex work where the trail has to be auditable later, like a big port or migration (the **show-me-your-work** skill).

Spawn Comment Sicko. Act on accepted findings.

---
name: statechart
description: "Check a TLA+ model of a system that moves between states, such as a product flow, a protocol, or a service, and draw it as a Mermaid statechart. The report gives the shortest path to each state that breaks a rule. Use for /statechart, or to show a bug as a path through states."
disable-model-invocation: true
---

# Statechart

The chart shows how a system moves between states, in the words of the person who reads it. That person, the reader, decides whether the behavior is right.

## Run

Work in a scratch folder outside the repo. Write a TLA+ spec and its config. Then run:

```sh
<skill dir>/scripts/statechart SPEC.tla [--config FILE] [--view FILE] [--out DIR]
```

`scripts/statechart.ts` is TypeScript, so run it with a runtime that can execute TypeScript.

The first run installs TLC and Java with mise and needs the network.

## Write the spec

- Write each rule that the reader agrees to as an INVARIANT. A rule can be about a screen, a result, a stored value, or a message. If the model has no variable for a rule, add the variable. Never weaken a rule to make it hold.
- Write `Next` as a disjunction of the actions, such as `YouPressPlay \/ YouPressStop`. If you do not, TLC names every step `Next`.
- A state with no step out breaks `NoDeadlock`, also when it is a correct end state. When an INVARIANT or a PROPERTY already has that name, the rule is `CHECK_DEADLOCK`. Add to `Next` an action that is true only in the end states and changes nothing, such as `Done == phase \in {"paid", "failed"} /\ UNCHANGED vars`, and give it a label in `step()`.

## Pick the chart

You do the work that needs judgment: the words on each state and arrow, the phases and their colors, the title, and the report to the reader. Put your work in a view module, and give it with `--view`.

To show the reader's words, the view exports `state(vars)`. The value that `state()` returns picks the form:

- A string gives a flat chart: `export const state = (v) => (v.paid ? "Paid" : "Paying");`
- An array gives parent states: `export const state = (v) => v.main.split(".");`
- An object gives one parallel region for each key: `export const state = (v) => ({ Playback: v.playback, Volume: v.volume });`

Label each state with what the reader can see or cares about, such as "Paying" or "Lease held, write pending". Keep variable names out of labels. In `vars`, a TLA+ sequence is an object with keys from 1, so `v.pc[1]` is `pc[1]`. A set is an array.

The view can also export `step(action, from, to)`. It gets the TLC action name and the values before and after the step, and it returns the label of the arrow. Write each step label as the user sees it happen, such as "you press play" or "the connect fails". Do not name the code or the TLA+ action. Two actions that end the same in the chart get the same label, so that they share one arrow.

When a step can occur only in some conditions, end its label with the condition in brackets, in the reader's words, such as `you press play [while the file loads]`. In a regions chart, the command writes the condition on the other regions on the arrow, in the words of their labels, such as `[when Offline]`. Your brackets replace it, and two arrows from one state can then look the same. So in a regions chart, do not write brackets for a condition on another region. When a value that no label shows decides where a step goes, name the result in the label, such as "the roster read fails".

The view can also export these:

- `group(vars)` returns the name of a phase. Each chart state gets the color of its group. When the model states behind one chart state are in different groups, that state gets no color.
- `colors` gives each group name a color class.
- `title` is a string that the chart shows at the top.

The command calls `state()` and `group()` at most once for each model state, and `step()` at most once for each step. The chart and the report both use those answers. So make each function depend only on its arguments.

The chart does not draw a step that stays in one label. Split a label when the reader must see such a step.

Aim for about 20 arrows or fewer, because a busier chart is hard to read. First return coarser labels from `state()`. Give one label to values that act the same, and leave out a detail that the reader does not need, such as a call in flight whose return changes nothing. Keep each state of a bug path, and keep each mark. When a merge changes a `breaks` state to `mayBreak`, it hides where a rule breaks. Do not merge two states that break different rules, because the reader then cannot see which rule breaks where. If the chart is still too busy, return `null` from `step()` for the steps that the reader does not need, such as a reset that every state has, or a step whose arrow repeats what other arrows show. Obey these rules when you hide steps:

- Keep each chart state reachable by arrows from a start state.
- Keep at least one arrow out of each chart state that has a step out in the model.
- Hide all the steps of an arrow, or none of them. When you hide only some, its condition gets narrower.
- In the hand-off, say which steps the chart hides.

## Read the report

- In the chart, a state that breaks a rule has the class `breaks`. When only some model states behind it break the rule, it has the class `mayBreak`. The Legend names the rules of each mark. When two rules break, it names both on one mark, so say in the hand-off which state breaks which rule. In a regions chart, a state gets a mark when each combination of region states that includes it can break a rule. When a combination can break a rule and none of its states has a mark, each state in that combination gets a mark.
- TLC goes past a state that breaks a rule, so the chart shows the states after a bug.
- Because TLC goes past bugs, a model with no limit on its states can run without end. Keep the constants small, or add a CONSTRAINT.
- With a VIEW or a SYMMETRY, TLC counts states that it treats as the same as one state, and the chart draws that one state. An arrow can lead to it rather than to the state that the step reaches, and the report says so.
- TLC checks the rules in each state past a CONSTRAINT or an ACTION_CONSTRAINT, but it does not explore that state or check it for deadlock. When TLC's shortest path for a rule ends in such a state, the chart draws that state, and the report gives that path. The chart does not draw the other states past the bound. A deadlock in such a state does not show. TLC also checks the rules after each step that an ACTION_CONSTRAINT excludes, also when it reaches the next state another way. When TLC's shortest path for a rule ends with such a step, the chart draws that step.
- The command checks the rules with TLC on the config as written, with one worker. When a rule breaks, the command removes that rule and runs TLC again, until no rule breaks. After the first break, each run stops at 100,000 distinct states, so that a large model does not run without end. When a run reaches that bound or stops on an error, the report lists the rules that it did not check under "Rules not checked", and the chart does not mark them. A rule that is not checked can hold or break. To check it, remove the rules that break from the config, or make the model smaller. The bound adds a module that changes TLC's order of the variables, so for a property TLC can find a different counterexample than a run without the bound.
- `tlc.out` is what TLC printed on the config as written. When the chart does not show the bug path of a rule that breaks, `tlc-RULE.out` is what TLC printed for the run that found it. When TLC repeats its first warning, plain TLC prints it twice, but `tlc.out` shows it once, because TLC leaves the second copy out of the output that this command reads. That happens only when Java runs with `-XX:+UseParallelGC`, since otherwise TLC's first warning is its advice to pass that flag, which it prints once.

## Show the chart

Show `chart.mmd` to the user as a `mermaid` code block. The chart has a budget of 500 states, counted by TLC on the config as written. Above that, the chart draws only the paths to the rules that break, and when no rule breaks, the command writes no `chart.mmd`. It still checks each rule, and the report gives the state count and each bug path. To see the whole graph, make the model smaller.

Render charts with Pele. When the user asks for an image, or a chart is too large to read as text, follow `references/render.md`. Do not use a different renderer unless the user asks for it.

## Hand off

Give each chart and its Mermaid text to the person who must decide. Add one line for each bug: the rule, the reader's sentence for that rule, and the path as the report numbers it. Say what the model leaves out. Give the command that makes the files again, with a new `--out` folder.

When the model describes code, replay each bug path against the real code, as a test or a live repro, one step for each action. If a bug does not occur, think that the model is wrong until you show that it is not.

# Create a verification skill

Every serious project needs a scripted way to drive the real app and prove behavior: launch it, exercise a feature the way a user would, and capture evidence. This skill generates that as a project-local skill (`.cursor/skills/verify-<app>/`) tailored to the repo. You write the generator's output for the next agent, not for a human: it will be read cold, mid-task, by an agent that has never seen the app.

## 1. Interview the repo, not the user

Answer these from the codebase and only ask the user what you cannot observe:

- **Surface:** what does a user actually touch? A web UI, a CLI/TUI, a desktop app, an API, a mobile app, a library? A repo can have several; pick the primary one and note the rest.
- **Run:** how does the app start locally? Prefer the repo's own documented dev command (package scripts, Makefile, README quickstart). Note ports, env vars, seed data, auth.
- **Drive:** how can an agent interact with it programmatically? Existing harnesses first — Playwright/Cypress specs, expect scripts, PTY helpers, curl-able endpoints, a debug port. Only then pick a generic recipe: browser/CDP for web and Electron, a tmux/PTY harness for CLI/TUI, plain HTTP for services.
- **Observe:** what evidence can be captured? Screenshots, terminal transcripts, response bodies, logs, exit codes, DB state.
- **Isolate:** can two instances run side by side (ports, data dirs, profiles)? If not, say so in the generated skill: refusing to double-drive a shared instance beats corrupting the user's session.

If the checkout doesn't build or start as-is, fix that first (or report it precisely) before generating; a skill written against a broken base teaches wrong steps. ---
name: show-me-your-work
description: "Keep a reviewable decision trail for long-running or unattended work: a TSV log with one row per decision (what, why, evidence, result). Local by default; commit it when a reviewer needs the trail to trust the result. Use for /show-me-your-work, autonomous or multi-phase runs, or work a human reviews after stepping away."
disable-model-invocation: true
---

# Show me your work

Keep one canonical log.

## The format

A single TSV file, one row per decision. Cells stay single-line. Evidence is a pointer, not prose.

Copy `references/decision-log-template.tsv` (the header row) to start a clean log. Columns:

- **ts.** ISO8601 timestamp.
- **phase.** The phase or workstream.
- **decision.** What was chosen or done, one line.
- **why.** The reason in plain words. If a principle drove it, say it plainly, not as a jargon tag.
- **evidence.** A link or path that proves it: commit SHA, PR number, `file:line`, or an artifact, trace, or screenshot path. Never a paragraph.
- **result.** The outcome or predicate state: `tests green`, `reverted`, `pixel-diff 0`, `INCONCLUSIVE`, `open`.

An example, plain-spoken so a reviewer reads it at a glance.

```
ts	phase	decision	why	evidence	result
2026-05-24T09:02:00Z	frame	counted the work first, about 100 components and roughly 75 hours	wanted to know the size before starting a long run	commit 3a9f1c2	found 5 things to sort out before starting
2026-05-24T09:40:00Z	harness	took screenshots of the old version before changing anything	so we can compare old against new and catch any visual change	scripts/snapshot.sh, baseline/	saved 120 reference screenshots
2026-05-24T11:15:00Z	widget	moved the widget styles over without changing how it looks	keep the change small and the result identical	commit 7c21e0a, pixel-diff 0	looks identical, tests pass
2026-05-24T12:30:00Z	widget	threw out a helper's work because its screenshots were blank	checked the real files instead of trusting its summary	worktree reset	reverted, tightened the instructions for next time
```

## Logging a row

Write each entry the way you'd tell a teammate what you did. Plain words, concrete actions, no AI speak or abstract jargon (the **unslop** skill applies to log text too).

Use the helper `scripts/log.sh <logfile> <phase> <decision> <why> <evidence> <result>`. It stamps `ts`, writes the header on first use, strips stray tabs/newlines, and prefixes any cell starting with `=`, `+`, `-`, or `@` with a single quote. A bare `printf` appending a row works too, but mind those same bytes if cells come from generated or user-supplied text.

Log decision points and checkpoints, not every action: a fork chosen, a unit completed with its verification result, a pivot or revert with its trigger, a blocker surfaced, a gate fixed. For loop runs, one row per iteration. Skip the trivial and self-evident.

A run is one agent conversation, including its later turns and any summary of it. A pickup, a replacement agent, or a new chat starts a new run. When a run adds to a log that already has rows, its first row has phase `start`, and so does its first row after another run's `start` row. So a run that comes back to a log in a later turn first reads the log's last rows to see whether another run wrote since. A `start` row names the `ts` range of the rows before it that this run did not write, and its evidence names this run, such as its agent id. Use phase `start` for nothing else.

## Where it lives

By default the log is a working artifact, not committed. Keep it at `decisions.tsv` in the work dir, or `.audit/<task-slug>.tsv` when several efforts run at once, and leave it out of git.

Commit it only when the work is ambitious enough that a reviewer needs the trail to trust the result.

## Rules

- Append-only. A wrong call gets a new row that supersedes it. Never edit or delete history.
- Prefer evidence produced by committed scripts over hand-made one-offs (the **encode-lessons-in-structure** principle skill).

## Audit the log against the transcript

At the end of the run, before handing back, check the log told the truth. Read this run's transcript under the active workspace's `agent-transcripts/` directory (the system prompt names the path). Don't glob across `~/.cursor/projects/*/`. That reads unrelated private chats. Walk this run's rows against what actually happened. Each stretch of them begins at one of this run's `start` rows, or at the first row if this run created the log, and ends at the next `start` row of another run:

- Check that every row maps to a real decision or action.
- Check that each row's evidence resolves and shows what the row claims.
- A fork, pivot, or abandoned approach that shaped the work but isn't logged is a gap. Add it.

Correct the log, not the story. The audit never edits or removes a row, even an invented one. When a row records neither a real decision nor a real action, or its claim or evidence is wrong, add a row that supersedes it with what actually happened and a pointer that resolves. This audit does not check rows outside this run's stretches. If this run's own work shows one of them is wrong, supersede it like any wrong call.

## Cross-model review of the trail

Before handing back, spawn a subagent on a different model family from the one that did the work. Self-review is not a substitute. The subagent reads the audit trail and the run's transcript, then flags what the user should pay attention to. Not a redo of the work, a scan for what's suboptimal or risky. Pick each subagent's reasoning level and fast or standard speed for the job, per the Subagents section of the **poteto-mode** skill.

- Decisions logged with weak or absent evidence.
- Verification steps skipped or claimed without proof in the transcript.
- Choices that look risky in hindsight (premature, scope-creeping, papering over a symptom).
- Gaps the user would otherwise miss on a casual skim.

Every reply for a run that produced a trail ends with an "Attention" section. Lead with the reviewer's model on its own line (`reviewed by <model>`), then list each flag pointing to specific rows or moments. "No flags" is a valid value. The model name is not.

## Reviewing the trail

Read top to bottom, follow the evidence pointers, spot-check. GitHub renders a committed TSV as a table. `column -s$'\t' -t decisions.tsv` renders it in a terminal.

## Composing this skill

Other skills route their audit trail here instead of inventing one. Reference it by name and let it own the format. Don't restate the columns.

Read-only audit of a test suite. Work in the git worktree C:\Users\mgsuk\.t3\worktrees\Moneo\t3-020838e5-de7d748e8ea1f495 (Windows, Git Bash available; Next.js + TypeScript, Vitest unit tests in `**/*.test.ts(x)`, Playwright specs in `e2e/`).

## Goal
The owner wants every test that would pass no matter what removed and replaced with a real one. Your job is to find them. I will do the rewriting, so I need a precise, verified list, not a long one.

A test "cannot fail" when breaking the behaviour it claims to check leaves it green. The usual causes:
- No assertion at all, or an assertion only inside a branch or callback that may never run.
- The expected value is computed by the code under test, or the assertion is on data the test built itself (asserting a mock returns what the test told it to return).
- The module under test is fully mocked, so only the mock is exercised.
- An assertion much looser than the claim (`toBeDefined`, `toBeTruthy`, `not.toThrow`, `toHaveBeenCalled` with no arguments checked) where the test name promises a specific result.
- A restated constant, prompt string or UI copy that never runs the code that uses it.
- A `try/catch` or `.catch(() => {})` in the test that swallows the failure, or an `expect` after an early `return`.
- `it.skip`, `test.skip`, `it.todo`, `describe.skip`, or a test body gated on an env var or fixture that is never present in `npm test`.

## Method
1. Enumerate cheaply first. For example: count `expect(` per test file; list test callbacks with zero `expect`/`assert` calls; grep for `toBeDefined|toBeTruthy|not.toThrow|toHaveBeenCalled()` and for skips. `git ls-files '*.test.ts' '*.test.tsx' 'e2e/*.spec.ts'` gives the file list (about 300 files).
2. Read the candidates and the code they test. Keep only the ones where you can name a concrete break of the behaviour that the test would not catch.
3. Prove the strongest ones by mutation: copy the repo's relevant source file to a temp name is NOT allowed, so instead make the one-line break in place, run only that test file with `npx vitest run <file> --testTimeout=60000`, record whether it still passes, then restore the file with `git checkout -- <file>` and confirm `git status --short` is clean before the next one. Do at most 15 mutation runs, on the candidates you are least sure about or that matter most (money math, auth, AI scopes, import/undo). Never leave a mutation in place.

## Rules
- Apart from those temporary one-line mutations, do not edit, create, commit, stash or push anything, and do not start subagents.
- Do not run the whole suite, Playwright, Docker, or anything against port 3000 or the network.
- The project's own test rules are in `AGENTS.md` under "Tests"; read that section. Tests that only assert UI copy, grep source files, or mirror the implementation are also unwanted there, so report those too, in a separate group.
- Skipped specs in `e2e/` that are skipped only because a backend is absent are expected; do not report them.

## Output
Plain text. Three groups, most important first within each:
1. **Cannot fail (proved by mutation)**: file:line, test name, the break you made, and that it stayed green.
2. **Cannot fail (verified by reading)**: file:line, test name, the concrete break it would miss, and why.
3. **Unwanted by the project's rules** (copy assertions, source greps, implementation mirrors): file:line, test name, one line why.
For each item in groups 1 and 2 add one line: what the test was meant to protect, and the assertion that would actually protect it (or "delete: already covered by <file:line>" when another test covers it).
End with the counts you enumerated (files, tests, tests with zero assertions, skips) and confirm `git status --short` is clean. Cap the list at 40 items; if there are more, say how many and what kind.

# Turn a correction into a check

Assume the next contributor is an agent that sees only the files it opened, copies the nearest example and takes the shortest path that compiles. A sentence in AGENTS.md is read sometimes; a check runs every time. The instruction is the symptom: change the code so the mistake cannot be made.

This applies to the product as well. When the assistant in the app gets a request wrong, a sentence in its system prompt (`lib/ai/provider.ts`, `lib/ai/voice-*`) naming that request is the same symptom fix. See step 2.

## Steps

1. **Name the class, not the case.** State the rule in one sentence with its reason. Then find every other place with the same fault: grep for the pattern, and check recent commits, reverts and review comments for earlier instances. If you cannot say why it matters, ask the owner before building anything.
2. **Fix it at the highest level that works**, in this order:
   - **Design.** Give each piece of state one owner and each job one supported way. Replace hand-synced lists with one source of truth. Delete the old way and any dead code an agent would copy. For the in-app assistant: give it the tool, the data or the scope it lacked, so this request and every similar one works.
   - **A type.** Make the wrong code fail to compile: a required parameter instead of a default, a narrowed or branded type, a function that only accepts the safe input.

Add a rule to the `moneo` plugin only when a selector cannot express it.
   - **A test**, when the rule is about behaviour. Follow AGENTS.md Tests.
   - **Prose in AGENTS.md**, last, only for judgment calls. Nothing fails when an agent skips it.

   In your reply, say which level you picked and why the one above it did not work.
3. **Write the error for an agent.** It says what is wrong, why, and the file, type or function to use instead, and it names the AGENTS.md section. "Don't do X" alone gets an `eslint-disable`.
4. **Fix every existing violation in the same change.** A rule with a pile of disables teaches that disabling is normal. If there are too many, scope the rule to the folders that are already clean, or make it fail only when a change adds more, and open an issue for the rest.
5. **Prove the check fails on the real mistake.** Reproduce the original mistake (the old line, the old import) and watch the check reject it; then confirm the fixed code passes.
   `printf '%s\n' 'import { a } from "@/app/page"; export const b = a;' | npx eslint --stdin --stdin-filename lib/sample.ts`
   Two config blocks that match one file replace each other's options for the same rule, so try a file from every folder the rule should cover.
6. **Update the rule table** in AGENTS.md ("Rules and what enforces them"): add the rule with its check. If the rule was there as a sentence, replace the sentence with the table row. Remove a row once the mistake can no longer be written at all.
7. Run `npm run lint`, `npm run typecheck` and `npm test`.

- Add a sentence to a system prompt that names one request, keyword or example to make that one case work.
- Write a check that greps source text or asserts copy.
- Encode a one-off preference about this diff. If it will not recur, just fix the code.

description: Draw the state machine of a Moneo flow as a diagram the owner can review, taken from the code, and list the paths that break a rule. # Draw a flow's state machine

The owner decides whether the behaviour is right, so the chart is in their words. Build it from the code, never from memory of how the flow should work.

## Steps

1. **Write the rules first.** List what must always hold, in sentences the owner would agree with: "an order is sent at most once", "undo puts back exactly what the import added", "nothing is written until the card is accepted". These are what the chart is checked against.
2. **Find where the state lives.** Usually a status column in `lib/schema.ts` (and its check constraint in `supabase/migrations/`), a union type, or a workflow in `workflows/`. List every value it can take.
3. **Find every transition.** Grep for each write to that status and each place it is compared. For each one record: from, to, what triggers it and the file and line.
4. **Walk it for holes.** Answer each from the code:
   - Is every state reachable, and can every state that is not final be left?
   - What happens on failure, on a second tap, and when two devices act at once?
   - What do undo, disconnect and "reset all data" do from each state?
   - What happens if the app quits mid-transition and starts again?

   For each rule from step 1, look for the shortest path of steps that breaks it. A question the code does not answer is a finding. Never weaken a rule or tidy the chart to hide one.
5. **Draw it** as Mermaid `stateDiagram-v2`.
   - Label a state with what the owner sees or cares about ("Reviewing", "Order sent, answer unknown"), not a variable name. Add the stored value in brackets only when it helps.
   - Label an arrow with the step as the owner sees it happen: "you confirm", "the bank says no", "Moneo restarts". Not a function name.
   - Mark the arrows the AI triggers and the ones that need an accepted card.
   - Aim for 20 arrows or fewer. Merge states that behave the same; never merge two states that break different rules.
   - Give every state that breaks a rule the class `breaks`.

   ```mermaid
   stateDiagram-v2
     classDef breaks fill:#fde2e2,stroke:#b42318
     [*] --> Uploaded
     Uploaded --> Reviewing: columns recognised
     Uploaded --> Failed: file unreadable
     Reviewing --> Imported: you confirm
     Imported --> Uploaded: you undo
     Reviewing --> Stuck: Moneo restarts
     class Stuck breaks
   ```

6. **Replay each broken path against the real code.** Write it as a failing test or a live repro, one step per arrow. If the bug does not happen, assume the chart is wrong until you show it is not.
7. **Hand it over.** In the PR description or in chat (rendered, not as source, when a preview tool is available): the chart, one line per broken rule with its path, and what the chart leaves out. When a change alters a flow, show the chart before and after.

## Do not

- Commit the chart to the repo. It goes stale like a comment; draw it again from the code.
- Invent states or transitions to make the picture tidy.

name: verify-ui
description: Prove a Moneo change works by driving the real QA app the way the owner would, and attach the evidence (screenshots in light, dark and mobile, or a recording) to the pull request. Use after any change to a page, component, style or user flow, when asked to "verify", "show me it works" or "add screenshots", and before opening a PR that changes what the owner sees.
---

# Verify a change in the running app

The owner reviews what the app does, not the diff. "It compiles" and "the tests pass" are not proof; pictures and recordings of the real app are.

Everything here runs against the QA app on http://localhost:3100. Never use port 3000; that is the owner's app and data.

## 1. Launch

`npm run setup -- --qa`, then `npm run qa:auth`, then `npm run qa:server` in the background. It is ready when `curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}" -H "x-moneo-test: 1" http://localhost:3100/api/health` prints 401 or 200.

If port 3100 is already taken, another checkout's QA app owns it and serves that checkout's code. Do not kill it. Start this checkout's app on a free port and point the tools at it with `E2E_BASE_URL=http://localhost:<port>`.

## 2. Doctor

Run this whenever anything looks off, before changing code:

`npm run qa:shots -- doctor home`

It fails with the reason when the app is not worth driving:

- **"The QA session was not accepted"**: the saved session expired (they last an hour). Run `npm run qa:auth`.
- **Every page is the "could not sign you in" screen after a fresh `qa:auth`**: the shared QA workspace holds data this checkout cannot read. Run `npm run qa:reset`.
- **A failed request or console error on an untouched page**: the base is broken. Fix or report that first; evidence taken on a broken base proves nothing.

## 3. Drive

1. **List the pages.** Every route the change can affect, including the ones AGENTS.md "Hit every surface" names. `npm run qa:shots -- <label> all` shoots every page in `lib/all-pages.ts`.
2. **Set up the state.** If a page needs data, create it the way the nearest spec in `e2e/` does. An empty page proves an empty page.
3. **Before.** With the change set aside (a temporary commit on another branch, or `git worktree add` of the base):
   `npm run qa:shots -- before home money/transactions`
   Name pages without the leading slash (Git Bash rewrites `/paths`); `home` is `/`.
4. **After.** On the changed code, the same command with `after`.

Each run writes `<page>-light.png`, `<page>-dark.png` and `<page>-mobile.png` to `.qa/shots/<label>/`, prints the HTTP status and every failed request or console error per page, and exits 1 if there were any.

**A flow, not a page.** A screenshot cannot show a tap, a card being accepted or an undo. Extend the journey spec in `e2e/` that already covers the flow and record it:

`npx playwright test e2e/<spec> --workers=1 --trace on --video on`

Add a new spec only when no existing journey can take the check (AGENTS.md Tests).

## 4. Evidence

- Use the path the owner uses: real pages, real buttons. Not a test-only endpoint or a direct database write for the step under test.
- Capture the action and the state it leaves, not only the last screen.
- Check the side effects next to what is visible: the row written, the history entry, what undo restores.
- **Look at every picture yourself.** Read each PNG. Check for overflow, clipped text, unreadable contrast in dark and a broken layout on mobile. A console error or a status of 400 or more is a failure: fix it and shoot again.
- When something looks wrong, suspect the capture before the app, and measure the live page before reporting a bug.

## 5. Hand over

Put before and after side by side in the PR description for each page that visibly changed, with one line on what to look at. Attach the video for a flow. Upload by dragging the files into the PR on GitHub, or ask the owner to if you cannot; `.qa/` is git-ignored, so never commit them. Say which pages you covered, what changed in each and what you could not capture and why. If nothing visibly changed, say so and attach nothing.

## 6. Clean up

Stop only the server you started, found by its port and this checkout's path, never by name. Leave `.qa/shots/` in place: cleanup removes instances, never the evidence.

- **Port line:** made true instead of softened. `lib/env.ts` now owns the app's address and lint rejects a hard-coded 3000 anywhere else.
- **"Could not sign you in" from an unreadable setting:** fixed. Readable preferences are kept and the rest fall back to defaults, with a test.
- **Sidebar covering content:** not a real bug. I measured the live page and it was an artefact of how the screenshot was taken; the screenshot command now freezes transitions.
- **Tests that could not fail:** an agent broke the behaviour behind suspicious tests and four stayed green (the ChatGPT sign-in verifier, the AI-label calibration reason, the "rows were cut" notice, the import confirmation). I rewrote each and confirmed three now fail on that break. The fourth was a redundant loose assertion, tightened but not re-broken.
- **Scheduled routes:** seven routes each copied the secret check. They now share one wrapper with a constant-time comparison, and a test walks every route and fails if one answers without the secret.
- **Database client:** one way to get a service-role client; lint rejects the raw form.
- **Workflows:** the four places that ignore a failure on purpose now call a function named for what handles it, since the explaining comments are gone. Lint rejects an unnamed empty catch there.

I pushed a fix: the job now retries starting the backend up to four times with a pause, since setup is safe to rerun. CI is running again on that commit and I'm still watching it.
